title: Updating twice
objectives: Chain two updates, using the first posterior as the next prior
Show that the order of independent evidence does not matter
Recognise evidence that is not independent

screens.prose: Your first test for the rare condition was positive, so your chance is now $\tfrac{2}{13} \approx 0.154$. You take a second, independent test. It is positive too.
screens.question: What is your chance of having the condition now? Give a decimal.

hints.text: The tree starts from your chance after the first test.
These two paths end in a second positive.
$\tfrac{2}{13} \times 0.9 \approx 0.1385$ and $\tfrac{11}{13} \times 0.05 \approx 0.0423$. Divide the first by their sum.

feedback.correct: About 0.77: the second positive moved you a long way.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run Bayes' rule again, starting from $\tfrac{2}{13}$.

byKey.stuck: That is your chance after the first test. The second positive is new evidence.
byKey.hit: That is the test's detection rate. Weigh it against the healthy path.
byKey.joint: That is condition and second positive together. Divide by both positive paths.

explain.text: $\dfrac{0.1385}{0.1385 + 0.0423} \approx 0.766$. The answer after the first test became the starting point for the second.

screens.prose: Two tests, two jumps on the log-odds line. Each arrow multiplies the odds by that test's likelihood ratio.
screens.question: Set the first ratio to 18 and the second to 4. Then swap them. Where does the end point land?

options.text: In the same place
Further right when the big ratio comes last
options.why: Try it: the end point does not move. Multiplying by 18 then 4 gives the same as 4 then 18.

options.text: Further left when the big ratio comes last
options.why: Try it: the end point does not move. The two jumps just swap places.

hints.text: Read the caption before and after the swap.
Watch the end point as you swap the ratios.

feedback.correct: The jumps add, so their order does not matter.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Swap the two ratios and watch the end point.

explain.text: 18 then 4, or 4 then 18: the odds are multiplied by 72 either way. On the line the two jumps simply swap places. The order of the evidence does not matter.

screens.prose: Using the first answer as the starting point for the second test is called **updating twice**. In odds it is two multiplications.
screens.question: Start at odds of $\tfrac{1}{99}$ and multiply by 18 for each positive. What are the odds after both? Give a decimal.

hints.text: Multiply, then multiply again.
Each arrow is one multiplication by 18.
$\tfrac{1}{99} \times 18 \times 18 = \tfrac{324}{99}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the odds by 18 twice.

byKey.added: You added the two ratios, $18 + 18 = 36$. Each test multiplies the odds.
byKey.once: That is after one positive. Multiply by 18 again for the second.
byKey.lr: You multiplied the ratios but left out the starting odds of $\tfrac{1}{99}$.

explain.text: $\tfrac{1}{99} \times 18 \times 18 = \tfrac{324}{99}$, so $p = \tfrac{324}{423} \approx 0.766$. That matches the tree on the first screen.

screens.prose: Same condition: base rate 1%, odds $\tfrac{1}{99}$. The first test is positive. The second comes back negative. The test misses 10% of cases and clears 95% of healthy people.
screens.question: What is your chance of having the condition now? Give a decimal.

widget.label: Chance after a positive then a negative

hints.text: What is the likelihood ratio of a negative result?
A negative has ratio $0.1 / 0.95 = \tfrac{2}{19}$. Odds: $\tfrac{1}{99} \times 18 \times \tfrac{2}{19} = \tfrac{4}{209}$, then $p = \tfrac{4}{213}$.

feedback.correct: About 0.019: the negative almost undid the positive.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the odds by 18, then by the negative's ratio $\tfrac{0.1}{0.95}$.

byKey.base: You assumed a negative exactly cancels a positive. Their ratios are 18 and about 0.105, which multiply to about 1.9.
byKey.ignored: That is the chance after the positive alone. The negative is evidence too.
byKey.miss: That is the test's miss rate. Use it to build the negative's likelihood ratio.

explain.text: A negative has likelihood ratio $\tfrac{0.1}{0.95} = \tfrac{2}{19}$. Odds become $\tfrac{1}{99} \times 18 \times \tfrac{2}{19} = \tfrac{4}{209}$, so $p \approx 0.019$. The positive and negative nearly cancel, leaving you just above the 1% base rate.

screens.prose: Same two results, but the negative test came back first and the positive second.
screens.question: How does your final chance compare with the last screen's 0.019?

options.text: It is exactly the same
It is higher, because the positive came last
options.why: The latest result has no extra weight. The odds meet the same two ratios, $\tfrac{2}{19}$ and 18.

options.text: It is lower, because the negative came first
options.why: Starting with the negative makes the middle step lower, but the second jump is the same size.

options.text: It cannot be found without redoing the tree
options.why: Multiplying the same two ratios in the other order gives the same product.

hints.text: Which two numbers multiply the starting odds?
$\tfrac{1}{99} \times \tfrac{2}{19} \times 18 = \tfrac{1}{99} \times 18 \times \tfrac{2}{19}$.

feedback.correct: The same two ratios, in either order, give the same answer.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two products of ratios.

explain.text: Multiplication does not care about order: $\tfrac{2}{19} \times 18 = 18 \times \tfrac{2}{19}$. On the line the two jumps swap places and land at the same point.

screens.prose: Now treat “two positives” as a single piece of evidence. With the condition it happens $0.9 \times 0.9 = 0.81$ of the time. Without, $0.05 \times 0.05 = 0.0025$.
screens.question: What is the likelihood ratio of “two positives”?

hints.text: A likelihood ratio is the chance of the evidence with the condition over the chance without.

byKey.once: That is the ratio for one positive. Two positives together are much stronger.
byKey.added: You added two ratios of 18. Divide 0.81 by 0.0025 instead.
byKey.diff: You divided 0.81 by 0.05. Both tests must be positive in the healthy case too: 0.0025.

explain.text: $\tfrac{0.81}{0.0025} = 324 = 18 \times 18$. One update with the joint evidence lands where two updates did. That works because the tests err independently.

screens.prose: Back to two positives on the 1% condition. Four people work out the chance after the second positive.
screens.question: Which answer is right?

options.text: $0.154$: Bayes' rule again from the 1% base rate
options.why: You started the second update from 1% again. That throws away the first positive.

options.text: $0.766$: Bayes' rule again from $\tfrac{2}{13}$
$0.81$: both tests catch the condition, $0.9 \times 0.9$
options.why: That is the chance of two positives given the condition. It leaves out the base rate and the false positives.

options.text: $0.024$: the first answer squared, $0.154^2$
options.why: Squaring a probability treats the two answers as separate events that must both happen. Update the odds instead.

hints.text: What should the starting point of the second update be?
After one positive you stand here, not at the start.
Run Bayes' rule from $\tfrac{2}{13}$, or multiply the odds $\tfrac{18}{99}$ by 18 again.

feedback.correct: The posterior from test one is the prior for test two.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start the second update where the first one ended.

byKey.old-prior: You reused the original 1% prior for the second test. That is the most common slip. The first positive already moved you to $\tfrac{2}{13}$, so start there.

explain.text: After one positive you stand at $\tfrac{2}{13}$. The second update starts there and lands at about 0.766. Restarting from 1% would land you back at 0.154, as if the first test never happened.

screens.prose: Write $O_0$ for the prior odds and $\text{LR}_1$, $\text{LR}_2$ for the two tests' likelihood ratios. Assume the tests err independently, both with and without the condition.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Start with the first update.

lines.text: $O_1 = \text{LR}_1 \times O_0$: the first result updates the prior odds
$O_2 = \text{LR}_2 \times O_1$: the first posterior is the second prior
$O_2 = \text{LR}_1 \times \text{LR}_2 \times O_0$: substitute the first line into the second

$	ext{LR}_1 \, 	ext{LR}_2 = \dfrac{P(E_1 \mid H)\,P(E_2 \mid H)}{P(E_1 \mid 
eg H)\,P(E_2 \mid 
eg H)} = \dfrac{P(E_1 \cap E_2 \mid H)}{P(E_1 \cap E_2 \mid 
eg H)}$: independent errors make this the ratio of both results together

hints.text: Which line needs $O_1$ to exist already?
First update, second update, substitute, then interpret the product.

feedback.correct: Two updates collapse into one, with the ratios multiplied.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line uses the one before it.

byKey.c2: The second update needs $O_1$, so the first update comes first.
byKey.c3: Substituting needs both updates written down first.
byKey.c4: Reading the product as one joint ratio comes last.

explain.text: Chaining the two updates multiplies the ratios. When the tests err independently, that product is exactly the ratio for both results at once. So two small updates and one big update agree.

screens.prose: Two analysts call a stock's direction. Each is right 70% of the time, whichever way it goes, and they work independently. You start at 50%. Both say up.
screens.question: What is the chance the stock goes up? Give a decimal.

widget.label: Chance of up given two up calls

hints.text: How likely are two up calls if the stock goes up? If it goes down?
Both these paths end in two up calls.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weigh both-right against both-wrong.

byKey.one: That is one analyst's call. The second independent call adds more.
byKey.joint: That is up with both calls up, out of everything. Divide by every way both say up.
byKey.either: That is the chance at least one is right. You need the chance of up given both say up.

explain.text: Each call has likelihood ratio $\tfrac{0.7}{0.3} = \tfrac{7}{3}$. Two calls: odds $1 \times \tfrac{49}{9}$, so $p = \tfrac{49}{58} \approx 0.845$. The tree gives the same: $0.49 / 0.58$.

screens.prose: Now you learn that analyst B reads A's note first and always copies A's call. Both say up. You start at 50%.
screens.question: What is the chance the stock goes up?

options.text: $0.7$: one analyst's worth
$0.845$: two calls' worth
options.why: That counts the same call twice. B adds nothing that A did not already tell you.

options.text: $0.5$: the calls cancel out
options.why: A's call is still real evidence with ratio $\tfrac{7}{3}$. Only B's copy adds nothing.

options.text: $0.91$: agreement makes it surer
options.why: Agreement only helps when it is independent. A copy always agrees.

hints.text: If you already know A's call, does B's call tell you anything new?
B's call is fixed by A's, so its likelihood ratio is 1. Update once, by $\tfrac{7}{3}$.

feedback.correct: A copy is not a second piece of evidence.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what B's call adds once you know A's.

explain.text: B's call is certain to match A's whatever the stock does, so it has likelihood ratio 1. Only A moves you: odds $\tfrac{7}{3}$, so $p = 0.7$. Correlated sources count for less than their number.

ideas: The posterior after one piece of evidence is the prior for the next.
For independent evidence the likelihood ratios multiply, in any order, and match one update on everything together.
Ratios that multiply to 1 cancel; correlated evidence counts for less than its number.

formula.name: Updating twice
formula.note: Valid when the two pieces of evidence err independently given $H$ and given $\neg H$.

summary.trap: Restarting the second update from the original prior throws the first result away; counting the same evidence twice inflates it.

quiz.prose: You give a takeover a 20% chance. One report has likelihood ratio 2, and a second, independent report has likelihood ratio 3.
quiz.question: What is your probability after both? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the odds by both ratios.

byKey.probs: You multiplied the probability 0.2 by 6. Multiply the odds instead.
byKey.first-only: That uses only the first report. Multiply by the second ratio too.
byKey.second-only: That uses only the second report. Multiply by the first ratio too.

explain.text: Odds $\tfrac{0.2}{0.8} = \tfrac{1}{4}$. Times 2 and times 3 gives 1.5, so $p = \tfrac{1.5}{2.5} = 0.6$.

quiz.prose: You give a stock a 30% chance of a dividend cut. One rumour has likelihood ratio 4. A later, independent rumour has likelihood ratio $\tfrac{1}{4}$.
quiz.question: What is your chance after both rumours?

options.text: $0.3$, where you started
Higher than 0.3, because the first rumour was strong
options.why: The second ratio is exactly the reverse of the first. The product is 1.

options.text: Lower than 0.3, because the last rumour counts most
options.why: Order does not matter. The two ratios multiply to 1.

options.text: $0.5$, because the evidence is split
options.why: Contradictory evidence cancels; it does not push you to 50%.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the two ratios.

explain.text: The two ratios multiply to $4 \times \tfrac{1}{4} = 1$, so the odds end where they started. Evidence that cancels leaves you at 0.3, not at 0.5.

quiz.prose: A lab runs your single blood sample through the same machine twice. Both readings are positive. A fault in the sample would fool the machine both times.
quiz.question: How should you treat the two readings?

options.text: As little more than one positive
As two independent positives: multiply by the ratio twice
options.why: Both readings share the same sample and the same machine. Whatever fooled one fooled the other.

options.text: As no evidence, since they agree
options.why: The first reading is real evidence. Only the repeat adds little.

options.text: As the average of the two readings
options.why: Evidence is not averaged. The question is how much the repeat adds, and here it is very little.

feedback.correct: A repeat on the same sample is not independent evidence.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the second reading could disagree with the first.

explain.text: Multiplying by the ratio twice assumes the two results err independently. Here they share every source of error, so the repeat adds almost nothing. Counting it twice is double-counting.
